cards.title: Introduction to Watchers
cards.content:
In Vue.js, watchers allow you to perform side effects in reaction to data changes. Unlike computed properties, which are used for synchronous derivations, watchers are ideal for asynchronous operations, costly tasks, or reacting to API calls.

import { ref, watch } from 'vue';

const count = ref(0);

watch(count, (newValue, oldValue) => {
  console.log(`Count changed from ${oldValue} to ${newValue}`);
});

options.text: Watchers are designed for side effects and asynchronous operations, while computed properties are for synchronous value derivation.
Computed properties can handle asynchronous API requests automatically.
Watchers cache their results, whereas computed properties run on every render.
There is no difference between them; they are aliases for the same feature.

cards.title: Deep Watchers and Immediate Execution
cards.content:
By default, watchers are shallow: they only trigger when the watched ref or getter changes. To watch nested properties inside objects or arrays, you need the deep: true option.

You can also use immediate: true to trigger the callback right away upon component creation.

const state = ref({ count: 0 });

watch(state, (newValue) => {
  console.log('State changed!', newValue);
}, { deep: true, immediate: true });

cards.title: Configuring Watcher Options
cards.content: To watch nested mutations in an object with watch(), you must pass the { ____: true } option as the third argument.

cards.title: Introduction to watchEffect
cards.content:
watchEffect() allows you to reactively track a function's dependencies automatically. It runs immediately on creation and automatically tracks any reactive properties accessed synchronously inside its callback.

import { ref, watchEffect } from 'vue';

const userId = ref(1);

watchEffect(() => {
  // Automatically tracks userId.value
  fetchUserData(userId.value);
});
